text: A cluster sized right for one workload shape can be badly wrong for another, even at the same core count. Sizing has to start from what the job actually does — shuffle-heavy or scan-heavy — not a generic instance-size guess.
Shuffle-heavy work bottlenecks on network and disk moving data between nodes. Scan-heavy work bottlenecks on raw parallelism, where node count matters more than per-node memory.

min_workers protects against cold-start latency; max_workers protects against a runaway job scaling out to consume far more budget than intended. Both should reflect typical load and worst tolerable load.

A bigger cluster helps genuinely parallelizable work. It does nothing when the real bottleneck is one severely skewed partition — that task still runs alone on one core no matter how many other cores sit idle.
Size for the workload's real shape, set autoscaling bounds around real load, and know when more nodes simply can't help. Next up: turning right-sizing into an actual cost story.
